newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Close race seen in Liberia poll as votes counted.
newsitem.headline: Close race seen in Liberia poll as votes counted.

text.p: Former Liberian warlord Charles Taylor prayed in church on Sunday with supporters who expect him to win elections to end the civil war he launched seven years ago.

But with only a fraction of the votes counted, Liberians waited to see whether he would win outright or be forced into an August 2 run-off -- most likely against former U.N. official Ellen Johnson-Sirleaf, the only woman among the 12 candidates.
"We do not know yet who has won the elections, but no one is going to win unless God wants him to," Taylor said at the Faith Healing Temple of Jesus Christ near Monrovia port.
"I believe in God," Taylor said to loud cheering from the partisan congregation after the regular service.
Liberians flocked to vote for a president and parliament on Saturday, suggesting a very high turnout.
Early assessments by counting agents suggested a close race between Taylor, 49, and Johnson-Sirleaf, 58.
A political party agent watching counting at elections headquarters said both polled well in the capital Monrovia.
The agent said the 10 other hopefuls were trailing in the Monrovia area. "We'll see how the other candidates do in their strongholds outside Monrovia," the agent added.
Taylor started civil war in 1989 but supporters and some opponents say his forceful character may embody the leadership quality needed in the immediate post-war period.
Johnson-Sirleaf entered the race late but built up support based on an image of integrity and good contacts with donors.
Taylor has vastly superior resources, including a national radio station, and ran a well-oiled electoral machine.
Liberian analysts say Johnson-Sirleaf could benefit from an anti-Taylor vote in any runoff. Two other former warlords, Alhaji Kromah and George Boley, were standing.
The elections commission has banned publication of unofficial results. Officials said it would issue partial returns for as much as 40 percent of the vote on Sunday.
Foreign experts said ballot boxes were still being retrieved from jungle locations by helicopters and human porters.
One expert said only 93 of about 1,900 ballot boxes had been counted. "We're talking of bringing them by canoe in some cases. We're talking of people carrying them on their heads," he said.
Officials expected about 60 percent of all boxes to be brought to Monrovia from polling centres by Sunday.
International monitors and Liberia's West African neighbours, who finally rallied the warlords around a peace deal, praised the smooth conduct of the poll.
"The process was smooth, hitch-free and devoid of rancour," Nigerian Foreign Minister Tom Ikimi told a news conference on behalf of a West African committee on Liberia.
Ikimi said he and foreign ministers of Ivory Coast, Guinea and Ghana observed voting in Monrovia and in the interior.

U.S. Senator Paul Simon headed an international monitoring team at elections in Croatia four weeks ago. "The election here yesterday, in every respect was at least as good or superior to the election in Croatia," he told a news conference.

More than 500 international observers, including former U.S. president Jimmy Carter, were in Liberia, underlying the determination of foreign donors, the United Nations and African states to head off election disputes.
Ikimi said the new president would decide whether the Nigerian-led West African force policing Liberia since 1990 should stay longer than its six-month post-election mandate.
